title: Games will always be handcraft, even with AI
author: Aikoioio
selftext:
Games are handcraft. That doesn't change whether you use AI or not.  
  
Last night I built a content curator product in just 4 hours. But the game script I wrote (with AI help, of course) took two months. My game has been in dev for three weeks.  
  
You'll find that what players need is more emotionally demanding than what regular product users need. More nuanced. Emotion is everywhere in a game, because it's not a tool.  
  
Somehow I feel like games will always be handcraft, no matter when and how. I believe in the future of AI games, but I don't think that conflicts with handcraft.  
  
Curious if others feel the same, or if you think AI will eventually change this.

replies.author: AvengerDr
replies.body:
>  Do you teach completely unique work that you, yourself came up with? Or do you teach the same data structures and algorithms that I can be taught at any community college or even some grade schools?

Teaching and research are two of the main activities that a university professor performs. I am more of a researcher than I am a teacher. I mean, I do have several unique contributions (papers) I have published at venues in my field, that would qualify as completely unique works or ideas that I came up with, with various degrees of involvement from other collaborators. Otherwise they wouldn't have been published. At the same time, I do also teach stuff other people have done, of course.

But there is a difference. Research is typically publicly funded and thus expected to be in the public domain. We could discuss about the necessity of having private organisations act as academic editors and publishers but that's a separate matter.

An image I create or source code I can put on my website does not immediately give you the authority to use it. As a developer you will be familiar with the concept of licenses. There is code that you can freely look at but but not use commercially, like GPL licenses. Why should that not apply to art, if I decide so? Being on the internet does not give you the consent to use it for training. It should always have been opt-in to start with.

> And I don't think anyone can be a game dev without understanding how to develop games without AI first.

Let's not confuse words here though. The AI you really need for a game is not the same as generative AI. State machines, behaviour trees, etc. are algorithmic processes. They don't need to be trained on existing materials.

> especially computer science in europe of all places, as people who are afraid of/can't cut it in the real world where results matter.

It's a popular view. Having been in academia for half of my life, I feel it's much more difficult to cut it in academa (at least, if you want to reach a modicum of international recognition) than in other fields.

You don't simply need to be good at something, you need to be among the best. If you can't land a job in your super-specific academic field, it's not like there are that many other places you can try to apply to. In some cases it means having to go to other countries or completely abandon the career. 

So much of it also depends on luck. I would hope that in gamedev there is a more clear relationship between how good the game you have created it with its commercial success. In academia you can still be good and fail anyway.

> Let's not pretend you haven't had a nothingburger of some research paper yet still published it and got false kudos.

Sure, but real quality works "bubbles up" after years and years of simmering. Having stuff out there, even if negative results, can still help others in the future to not reinvent the wheel.

comments.author: Unusual-Marzipan5465
comments.body:
Building games pre-AI is like building a house by yourself. You need to know architecture, but also: carpentry, masonry, plumbing, and electrical engineering.

With AI, you have a carpenter, a mason, a plumber, and an electrical engineer. But you still need to be the architect. If you don't know how to build a house in general, you'll end up with a house that's no good to live in.

In the same way, you must be a game designer. You need to have a general idea of how game systems work, and what makes a game fun.

replies.author: Aikoioio
replies.body: Great analogy. All AI really does is stack layers on top of each other. It has no visual sense and no ability to experience a game. So everything needs to be tuned by a human, and human energy is limited. You end up going back and forth between system after system, debugging and adjusting. It's incredibly time consuming, but also really rewarding.

replies.author: daddywookie

I’m finding it funny as a Product Owner that a lot of the AI developer conversation is about similar issues to what I work with. How to maintain output standards, how to organise work, how to ensure value is created instead of volume, how to define problems clearly without restricting innovation.

There is plenty of space for designers, producers, QA and developers in the AI game dev world, they’ll all just have to learn to work with different tools and processes. For me, I’m trying to understand if Scrum can be converted to an AI centric workflow, what the core artefacts and ceremonies become and what the roles are.

comments.author: anaveragebest
comments.body:
My opinion is this: In the same way using a computer to type a book instead of writing it on paper, AI is a tool. AI cannot create art, and if your game is going to be an art and not a product, then AI can never produce it (not fully).

You may disagree with this. But the idea is pretty simple, we (humans) create art, and we grow from that. AI does not create an art, it creates copies. Copies (original or not) that itself does not care for or appreciate. No matter how good it gets at creating movies/film, art, or music, it will never truly be art. In the end when that creation has no human attachment, and no value to the thing that created it, it will always lack what defines something as art: meaning.

Although I think it can help you reach conclusions, it can help guide to a finished thing, and it can expedite the creation of idea making processes. I think of it only as a tool.

replies.author: Aikoioio
replies.body: I totally agree, "AI does not create an art, it creates copie". As a game designer who can't code, being able to immediately bring my ideas to life is genuinely exciting, even if it means spending more time fixing experience issues AI can't perceive, doing endless optimization work. Having this "soulless" development partner actually gives us more power than ever. And what we need to do is simply hold on to what makes us human: the relentless pursuit of art.

comments.author: code-garden
comments.body:
Right now I believe that human effort is required to produce interesting art. I think that part of the enjoyment of art comes from abstracted communication of ideas between artist and spectator. I think that AI is too different from the human mind for us to have the same sort of communication. Too much appears as unintentional mistakes which are difficult to understand from a human perspective, which creates a disconnect.

If AI starts to produce great art in a few years I may change my mind.

comments.author: daddywookie
comments.body:
I think the market is large enough and varied enough that hand crafted experiences can live alongside mass market AI products.

My wife is the very definition of casual-core. She has multiple casual games on her phone, and regularly deletes old ones and grabs new ones as she gets bored or hits scaling limits. She really doesn’t care how they are produced or even know how to find out. She plays, she watches ads, she moves on.

There is a huge market segment that isn’t noisy on Reddit complaining about “AI slop”. I can see studios forming with AI tooling to churn out dozens of casual-core games. The barest game idea will become a simple game loop with minimal lifespan and a million downloads on minimal margins.

For the “gamers” there will always be the hand crafted and lovingly sculpted experiences. These might arrive quicker with AI but they will always have the hand of their creator woven through them.

replies.author: Aikoioio
replies.body:
Yes, and I'm very much in the handcrafted camp as a player. FPS, Souls-likes, roguelikes. Those are my games.

But when I want to \*make\* something, say, a sci-fi apocalyptic metaphor built around the Tower of Babel, I'm glad coding agents exist. I use the best ones I can get (Codex → Claude → 1M Opus) to write the code. That doesn't make me less of a creator. I'm still me.

There's no conflict. The taste and joy I've built up from thousands of hours in handcrafted games, that's exactly what I bring to the table when I direct AI in my own workflow. The standard doesn't drop just because the tools changed.

comments.author: propnalysis

completely agree, the emotional intentionality behind every design decision is what separates a game from a product and ai cant manufacture that. even when ai handles the technical execution the vision, pacing, and "feel" still comes entirely from the human behind it.  
  
that said ai is genuinely amazing for collapsing the gap between idea and playable prototype, codewisp lets u describe ur game and generates a playable web game instantly which means more time spent on the handcraft parts that actually matter instead of fighting engine setup and boilerplate
